How far do the efficiency scores move with the prior?

Source: R/prior_sensitivity.R
prior_sensitivity.Rd

Refits a model across a grid of prior median efficiencies and reports how much the scores change, which is a direct measurement of the thing skewness_test tests a proxy for.

prior_sensitivity(
  object,
  r_star = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.9),
  keep_u = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

object

an object of class "sfmodel". Priors need not have been added; where they have, everything but the anchor is kept.

r_star

the prior median efficiencies to try, at least two.

keep_u

passed to add_posterior_coefficients. The scores need the draws, but an interval may be given to thin them.

verbose

whether to report progress, one message per fit.

Value

A list of class "sfsens", with efficiency, a data frame of the score summaries by anchor; coefficients, the posterior means of the frontier coefficients by anchor; spread, the range of the mean score; relative, that range over the spread of the scores between units, which is the figure to read; coef_spread; and the seed used throughout.

Details

The inefficiency term is the part of a frontier model the data speak to least, and its prior is expressed as an anchor, r_star, in the units of the response. Where the sample is informative the posterior barely notices the anchor; where it is not, the scores follow it. Since that difference decides whether the scores can be reported as findings, it is worth measuring rather than assuming, and it costs one refit per grid point.

This is the Bayesian form of the question. skewness_test asks whether the residuals carry the asymmetry a one-sided term would produce, which is a property of the data and needs no sampling, but is a test, with a test's error rate and its asymptotics. This asks what the anchor does to the answer, which is the quantity of interest itself and has no null distribution to get wrong. On a sample simulated with no inefficiency at all, the mean score moved by 0.036 as the anchor ran from 0.5 to 0.9, against 0.005 for a sample that had plenty; the skewness test called that same empty sample informative.

Read relative rather than spread. The movement of the mean matters in proportion to how far the scores are spread between units in the first place, and the absolute figure cannot tell a mean that moves a lot among tightly packed scores from one that moves a little among widely spread ones. Over fifteen simulated samples the absolute figure overlapped between the informative and the empty case; the relative one did not.

No threshold separates the two cleanly in every sample, and none should be expected to: where the one-sided term is about the size of the noise, the data genuinely do not pin the level down, and a middling figure is the honest answer rather than a failure of the diagnostic.

Every fit uses one seed, the model's own where it has one, so that the table shows the prior moving the answer rather than the sampler doing it. The rest of the prior specification is carried over unchanged, so a model that already has priors keeps them and varies only the anchor. For a four-component model both anchors, persistent and transient, move together.

The frontier coefficients are reported alongside, and are usually the reassurance: they hold still while the scores move, which is the pattern to expect and says the fitted frontier is not in question even where the distance to it is.

See also

skewness_test for the check that needs no sampling, add_priors for what the anchor means.

Examples

set.seed(1234)
d <- sim_sf(n = 200, beta = c(1, 0.5), sigma_v = 0.2, par_u = 4)

model <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1, data = d,
                            iterations = 500, burnin = 200)
prior_sensitivity(model, r_star = c(0.6, 0.9))
#> Sensitivity of the efficiency scores to the prior
#> 
#> Frontier:     production
#> Inefficiency: exponential
#> Seed:         1038071299 for every fit
#> 
#> Mean efficiency by prior median efficiency:
#>   r_star   mean     sd    min    max
#> 1    0.6 0.7921 0.1324 0.1762 0.9484
#> 2    0.9 0.8053 0.1243 0.1855 0.9492
#> 
#> Frontier coefficients:
#>     (Intercept)     x1
#> 0.6      1.0206 0.4957
#> 0.9      1.0003 0.4940
#> 
#>   scores move by  0.0131 across the grid
#>   that is         0.1 times their own spread across units
#>   coefficients by 0.0203 at most
#> 
#> The anchor moves the scores by little beside the spread between units,
#> so they are estimated from the data rather than carried over from the
#> prior.
#>
